title: Senior's toolkit: permissions and access
summary: namei, chmod with X and setgid, chown, sudo -l, usermod -aG, umask, ACLs and a setuid audit.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: permissions and access
steps.body: "Permission denied" is one of the most common tickets on a Linux box. These commands find which part of the path refuses, and fix it without reaching for `chmod 777`.

toolkit.what: Shows owner and permissions of every directory along a path. Finds the one folder without `x` that blocks access to a file deep inside.
toolkit.when: a file looks readable but access is still denied

toolkit.what: Sets permissions recursively in symbolic form. Capital `X` gives execute only to directories (and files that already had it), so files do not all become executable.
flags: setgid on a directory: new files inherit its group
toolkit.example: sudo chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /srv/app && sudo chmod g+s /srv/app

toolkit.what: Changes owner and group. Services should own only the folders they must write to, such as logs and uploads.
Lists what you are allowed to run with sudo on this machine. `sudo -u` runs a command as a service user, to reproduce its permissions exactly.
flags: a login shell as that user
toolkit.when: testing what a service account can really read

toolkit.what: Adds a user to an extra group. Without `-a` it replaces all their groups. The change applies at the next login.
flags: use the new group in the current shell
toolkit.example: sudo usermod -aG docker alice && id alice

toolkit.what: Sets the permissions removed from every new file and folder. `027` gives 640 files and 750 folders: nothing for other users.
flags: the same for a systemd service

toolkit.what: Access control lists: give one extra user or group access without changing the owner or opening it to everyone.
flags: default ACL inherited by new files
toolkit.example: sudo setfacl -R -m u:deploy:rwX /srv/app && sudo setfacl -d -m u:deploy:rwX /srv/app

toolkit.what: Lists setuid programs, which run as their owner (often root). A standard check in a security review.

steps.prompt: nginx returns 403 for `/home/alice/site/index.html`. The file is `-rw-r--r-- alice alice`. `sudo -u www-data cat` on it also fails. What do you run to find the cause?
options: `namei -l /home/alice/site/index.html`: a parent folder such as `/home/alice` (often 750) lacks `x` for others
steps.explain: To open a file you need `x` on every directory on the way. The file's own bits are fine; the home directory is not. Serve the site from `/srv` or `/var/www` instead of opening up a home directory.

steps.prompt: Match each mode to its meaning.
pairs: owner reads and writes, group reads, others nothing
a folder the owner manages and the group can enter
only the owner, for example an SSH private key
a shared folder whose new files keep the folder's group
a program that runs as its owner (setuid)

steps.prompt: Add alice to the `docker` group without removing her other groups.
steps.explain: `-G` alone sets the complete list of supplementary groups, so alice would lose `sudo` and every other group. `-g` changes her primary group.

steps.prompt: You ran `sudo usermod -aG docker alice`. `id alice` lists `docker`, but in alice's open terminal `docker ps` still says `permission denied ... /var/run/docker.sock`. Why?
options: Group membership is read at login; she must log in again (or run `newgrp docker`)
steps.explain: A process keeps the groups it started with. `id alice` reads the database; `id` with no argument in her shell shows the groups that shell really has. Membership of `docker` is effectively root access, so grant it with care.

items: The service writes logs but its log folder is owned by root
An SSH key is `-rw-r--r--` and ssh refuses it
A new developer must use Docker without sudo
Everyone in the web team should edit `/srv/site`
Only the `deploy` user needs write access to one app folder owned by `app`
A backup user needs read access without changing owner or group

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When access fails, reproduce it with `sudo -u <service-user>` and walk the path with `namei -l` before changing anything. Fix with the smallest grant that works (a group, an ACL, one folder's mode); `chmod 777` is a finding in every security review.
